slides.title: Pythagorean Theorem
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today the theorem runs forward: two sides of a right triangle find the third.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q4 is Notes III's move before it has a name: 10² − 6² = 64 = 8², the missing leg of the 6-8-10 triangle Notes II builds. Say that in one sentence after the reveal. Two minutes silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the theorem and the picture.
slides.note:
Mark the square corner first, every time: the side across from it is c, the hypotenuse, and it is the longest side. The other two are the legs, a and b, in either order. The theorem is not on the FAST sheet — it is memorized, and today it is on the board until it is. A triangle turned on its side has the same c: find the square corner, not the bottom (the state's named misconception is misidentifying the hypotenuse).
OFF: 'Find the square corner. The side across from it is c.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Legs 6 and 8: 36 + 64 = 100 and c = 10 — whole, because 6, 8, 10 is a Pythagorean triple. Legs 3 and 5: 9 + 25 = 34, and 34 is not a perfect square, so c = √34 exactly, between 5 and 6 (25 < 34 < 36), about 5.8. Leave √34 when the question wants the exact length; round to the tenth when it asks for a measurement, and round once, at the end.
OFF: 'Square, add, then the root. The root is the last step.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Hypotenuse 17, one leg 15: the 17 is c, so 17² stands alone and the 15 goes beside the unknown leg: a² + 225 = 289, a² = 64, a = 8. Check: 8 is shorter than 17, as a leg always is. A board that adds 225 + 289 gets about 22.7 — longer than the hypotenuse, impossible, and the check catches it (the book names adding as the error; the state names misidentifying the hypotenuse).
OFF: 'A leg is shorter than the hypotenuse. Always check.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask where the square corner is and which side is c before anyone squares.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: 49 + 81 = 130, not a perfect square: c = √130, between 11 and 12 (121 < 130 < 144), and 11.40 to two places, so 11.4. A board with 16 added the legs.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 25 + 121 = 146 and √146 ≈ 12.08, so 12.1 — a board with 16 added the legs; a board with 146 stopped before the root.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Ask which number is c before anyone squares: 15, the longest — so this time a square is subtracted.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: 15 is c, so 15² stands alone: b² + 64 = 225, b² = 161, b = √161 ≈ 12.69, so 12.7 — and 12.7 is shorter than 15, as a leg must be. A board with 17 added the squares (√289): a whole number, and longer than the hypotenuse.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 121 − 36 = 85 and √85 ≈ 9.22, so 9.2 — a board with 12.5 added the squares (√157), longer than the hypotenuse.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).
